transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-04-08
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (CTO), Jordan Miles (ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be fuzzy):
Kepler is evaluating hosting options for low-latency patient-facing summarization and triage prompts. Primary concerns: p95 latency under 350ms for short streaming responses, concurrency of ~150 sustained users with bursts to 1200, token/sec benchmarking for 512-token outputs, and enterprise requirements (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, fallback models, and pilot plan.

Topics:
- p95 targets & measurement methodology
- Streaming/partial response behavior and client-side UX
- Concurrency modeling and autoscale/burst strategy
- Private (VPC) deployment constraints and KMS integration
- Pilot scope: sample prompts, profiling, pricing

Action items: see metadata list above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. Maya is our systems SE who'll run the profiling.
[00:12] Priya (Kepler CTO): Hi -- Priya here. We're mainly focused on latency for our patient triage flow and also making sure we can handle concurrent consults.
[00:18] Jordan (Kepler ML): Jordan, ML eng. We'll be feeding the models with anonymized clinical notes, about 70 tokens in, 400-600 out for summary flows.
[00:26] Samir (Infra): Samir, infra. We need VPC peering and KMS, plus audit logs for compliance.
[00:32] Maya (Redwood SE): Great. Quick agenda: clarify p95 targets, traffic shape, whether streaming is required for UX, and then map to Hosted / Dedicated / Private options and a pilot.
[00:42] Priya: For short answers we want p95 sub-350ms ideally. For the long summaries p95 a bit looser, like under 800ms, but the main metric is the patient-facing triage questions where responsiveness matters.
[00:54] Alex: Cool. When you say sub-350ms, is that end-to-end client perceived latency including network, or service-to-service?
[00:59] Priya: End-to-end, yes. Browser to our app to model. But we know network is variable, so we need the inference portion to be around 200-250ms p95 for short streaming responses.
[01:10] Maya: That helps. What's your concurrency profile look like? Sustained QPS or user concurrency?
[01:16] Jordan: We model concurrent active sessions. Right now it's about 150 concurrent active users during peak, but we have traffic bursts for campaign events up to ~1,200 concurrent for a few minutes. Average session issues around 3-4 requests per session.
[01:28] Maya: OK so we need steady-state sizing and burst readiness. On Redwood Hosted we can provision autoscaling with burst lanes; Dedicated gives more predictable tail latency but needs commit. Private is the VPC/on‑prem route with more control but higher ops work.
[01:40] Samir: For compliance we prefer VPC peering + customer-managed KMS. We also need full audit logs stored for 2 years. Is that available on Hosted?
[01:49] Alex: Hosted supports SOC2 and we can integrate with external KMS in Dedicated and Private; Hosted has encrypted keys but not customer-managed KMS today unless we do a Dedicated/Private contract. Logs retention add-on is available. We can document options in the security pack.
[02:02] Priya: Good. On throughput: we want concrete tokens/sec numbers. For our largest summary prompt, roughly 512 tokens output, what kind of tokens/sec should we expect on your recommended model family?
[02:12] Maya: It depends a lot on choice of model (quantization, sequence length) and runtime. If you're using streaming with chunked tokens, we often see 15-40 tokens/sec on a single GPU for large models (vXX class), but optimized small-medium models can do 80-120 tokens/sec. For p95 we recommend profiling with your exact prompts — Maya will run profiling.
[02:32] Jordan: Are those numbers for continuous streaming or per-request end-to-end? I'm thinking of tokens/sec during generation.
[02:38] Maya: Yes tokens/sec during generation. Also batching and KV cache reuse matter. If you have repeated prefixes (like identical system prompts), prefix caching increases effective tokens/sec in production.
[02:49] Priya: We do have a heavy prefix in the triage flows — the patient context is appended but system prompt is consistent. How big of a difference does caching make at p95?
[02:58] Maya: Could be 20-40% lower latency on the token path when prefix caching hits, depending on sequence length. But cold starts and unique contexts will still pay the full cost.
[03:08] Alex: On Dedicated the advantage is we can reserve capacity so p95 is more predictable for cold-starts and concurrent bursts; Hosted is cheaper initially and fast to get going. Private gives your infra controls for keys and network but you take on ops.
[03:21] Samir: For pilot we prefer starting Hosted if we can meet latency targets, then move to Dedicated if needed — that minimizes procurement friction. Is that a common pattern?
[03:28] Alex: Yes, many customers do a hosted pilot, then commit to Dedicated after we validate p95 and concurrency. We'll provide a pilot pricing tier for sustained test traffic.
[03:35] Jordan: For benchmarking, we'd like to run a token/sec script. Maya, what do you need from us?
[03:40] Maya: Send 3 canonical prompt templates (short triage Q, medium follow-up, long summary) and a 7-day traffic histogram. I'll run them against a couple of model sizes in hosted preview to capture p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec and share the CSV.
[03:54] Priya: Timeline: can we get initial numbers by end of next week?
[03:58] Maya: Yes, if you share prompts by Friday the 11th I'll aim to return profiling by Sunday/Monday with notes.
[04:07] Samir: A few infra specifics — do you support VPC peering for Hosted or only Dedicated/Private? Also what's your data residency options?
[04:15] Alex: VPC peering is available for Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports region controls but not VPC peering for standard plans; we can discuss enterprise Hosted variants with private egress in the contract. Data residency: we can pin regions for Hosted; for strict residency you'd go Dedicated/Private.
[04:30] Jordan: About streaming — our front-end expects a streaming token every ~150ms to feel snappy. Does Redwood support chunked streaming with keepalive and partial outputs?
[04:39] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports SSE/HTTP chunking with incremental tokens and function-calling structured outputs. The client-perceived latency is often improved by early partial tokens even if final tokens take longer. There can be tradeoffs with network backpressure; we can recommend chunk sizes.
[04:52] Priya: Are there any caveats for p95 when streaming? Like does chunking increase p95 because of buffering?
[04:57] Maya: Potentially. If you wait to accumulate chunks on the server-side, that adds latency. Our recommendation is to stream as soon as tokens are produced. The p95 we measure for 'first token' is often much lower than 'full response' p95 for long outputs. We'll capture both metrics.
[05:12] Jordan: Cost sensitivity — do you have estimates for tokens-per-dollar for the models you recommend? We need to justify economics compared to our existing infra costs.
[05:20] Alex: We'll include cost per 1M tokens for hosted vs dedicated committed rates and show a break-even curve for your expected QPS. We can also outline batching and quantization levers to reduce unit cost.
[05:31] Priya: One more security point: we required SSO + RBAC for console access and audit trail exports.
[05:36] Alex: Yes Redwood supports SSO (SAML/OIDC) and role-based access, and audit exports can be included as an add-on.
[05:43] Samir: Any known limitations with model variants during fallback? We want graceful degradation to cheaper models during capacity constraints.
[05:49] Maya: We have routing policies for fallback sequences: you can configure a cost-fallback to a quantized or smaller model; we can run canary rollouts. The tradeoff is potential quality regression — we tie rollouts to evals to guard against surprises.
[06:02] Priya: Sounds good. For our pilot, let's do hosted profiling first. If p95 for the short triage is under 350ms end-to-end in typical infra we will move to a Dedicated committed lane to get better burst isolation.
[06:14] Alex: Perfect. I'll send the pilot contract and pricing options. Maya will run the profiling. Jordan will share prompts.
[06:20] Jordan: Quick clarifying note — our payloads include 150-200 tokens of patient notes in some flows, so effective sequence length can be 700-800 tokens total. That impacts kernel selection, right?
[06:29] Maya: Yes larger context windows push different kernels and can reduce tokens/sec. We'll capture both 512 and 800 token profiles. Also quantization effectiveness varies by context length.
[06:40] Priya: Any references you can share for measuring p95 properly? We want to align on methodology so we compare apples-to-apples.
[06:46] Maya: I'll share our throughput playbook and a profiling script (link: https://redwood.ai/docs/throughput-playbook) which includes generation of p50/p95, first-token vs full-response, and how to simulate concurrent bursts.
[06:58] Alex: Next steps recap: Alex share pilot pricing + security docs; Maya run profiling with provided prompts; Jordan provide prompts and traffic hist; schedule benchmark deep-dive next week.
[07:08] Priya: Thanks all. If profiling shows hosted won't meet the p95, we'll expect numbers to justify a Dedicated commit.
[07:15] Alex: Understood. Anything else before we close?
[07:18] Samir: One small ask — can audit logs be streamed to our S3 or do they need to be pulled?
[07:23] Alex: We can push logs to your S3 via a secure staging pipeline as part of the add-on. We'll include the details in the security doc.
[07:30] Priya: Cool. Thanks, talk soon.
[07:33] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items and a proposed time for the deep-dive.

End of transcript.
